html:
In 1937 the Soviet government forcibly moved nearly 172,000 Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia. It was the first deportation of a whole nationality in the Soviet Union.

Koreans had settled near Vladivostok since the 1860s, many fleeing hunger and later Japanese rule at home. With Japan at war in China, Stalin and Molotov ordered them removed, claiming they might spy for Japan. The secret police, the NKVD, loaded them onto 124 trains for a journey of over 6,000 kilometres. Many, especially children and the old, died on the way or in the first hard winter.

They were dumped on the steppes and in the oases of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. There they built collective farms and became known for rice and vegetable growing. Their descendants, the Koryo-saram, still live across the region. The deportation set a pattern later used on the Chechens, the Crimean Tatars and others.
sum: In 1937 the Soviet government forcibly moved nearly 172,000 Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia. It was the first deportation of a whole nationality in the Soviet Union.
